steps.ttsScript: When we write, we follow a few important rules.
The rules help our readers understand us.
Let us learn two big ones.
Every sentence starts with a capital letter.
The dog runs. See the big T?
Names also start with capitals. Maya, not maya.
Every sentence ends with a mark.
A period for telling. A question mark for asking. An exclamation mark for excited.
Pick the mark that fits your sentence!
Here is a helpful trick.
When you write, check the start and the end of every sentence.

displayParts.text: Check the start and the end

steps.ttsScript: Now you are ready to use capitals and periods!
Some words mean almost the same thing. But one is stronger!
Like paint colors. Some are soft. Some are super bright.
Words have shades too!
Big means something is large.
Huge means even bigger than big!
An elephant is big. A whale is huge!
steps.displayText: An elephant is big. A whale is huge!

steps.ttsScript: Happy means you feel good.
Thrilled means super, super happy!
A little smile, or a big jumping cheer. Different shades!
Here is a helpful trick.
Strong words paint a stronger picture. Pick the shade that fits!
Now you are ready to pick between strong and mild words!
Compound words are two words stuck together.
You can use both pieces to guess the meaning!
Rainbow! Rain plus bow.
A bow of color in the rain. Makes sense!
Sunflower. A flower that loves the sun.
Toothbrush. A brush for your teeth.
Here is a helpful trick.
See a long word? Look for two smaller words inside!
Now you are ready to read compound words!
Words can mean almost the same thing but have different strengths.
Like different shades of the same color.
Angry means upset.
Furious means very, very angry!
Happy. A small, warm feeling.
Joyful. A bigger, fuller feeling.
Thrilled. You are bursting with it!
Here is a helpful trick.
Ask: how strong is the feeling? Then pick the word that matches!
Now you are ready to pick the right shade of meaning!
Have you ever noticed that some words have similar meanings?
Some words have similar meanings but different strengths.
Today, we'll explore these different levels of word strength!
Hungry. A bit hungry.
Starving. Really hungry!
Famished. Extremely hungry!
Tired is normal.
Exhausted is way more.
These words show different levels of feeling tired.
Here is a helpful trick.
Match the strength of the word to the strength of the feeling.
Now you are ready to pick the right strength!
Style is the way you choose to write.
It's how you make your writing sound unique, just like your own voice!
Precise words paint clearer pictures.
Precise > vague
Good writers choose just the right words to make their stories shine.
Using precise words helps your reader imagine exactly what is happening.
For example, instead of 'walked,' you could say 'tiptoed' if someone was quiet.
Or, instead of 'said,' you might use 'whispered' if they spoke softly.
These precise words paint a clearer picture and make your writing more exciting!
Here is a helpful trick.
Match your style to your reader. Casual for friends. Formal for school.
Now you are ready to choose words for style!
Similes and metaphors compare two things to paint a picture.
This helps us understand ideas better and makes our writing more interesting!
A simile uses like or as.
As busy as a bee.
A metaphor says one thing IS another.
My heart is a star.
Here is a helpful trick.
See like or as? Simile. See is or are connecting unlike things? Metaphor.
Now you are ready for similes and metaphors!
Synonyms have shades of strength.
Think of it like colors. You can have light blue, blue, and dark blue. They're all blue, but with different strengths.
Today, we'll learn to identify these different levels of strength in words.
Glance is quick.
Look is normal.
Stare is intense!
Whisper is soft. Talk is normal. Yell is loud!
Here is a helpful trick.
Pick the word strength that matches the actual feeling.
Now you are ready for word strength levels!
Fact books are full of real things from our world.
They can be about anything! Animals, space, weather, food.
Let us learn how to read fact books all year.
Pick fact books about things you love.
Love bugs? Read about insects. Love space? Read about planets.
You will have so much more fun when it is your favorite topic.
Fact books have helpers built in.
Headings. Pictures. Labels. Use them to find facts fast.
They are like a roadmap through the book!
Here is a helpful trick.
Try a new topic each week. You will discover something you did not know!
Now you are ready to explore fact books all year!
Fact books give us two kinds of clues.
The words tell us facts.
The pictures show us how it looks.
Today, we will learn how words and pictures give us different kinds of information in a book.
Look at this book about ladybugs; the words tell us that ladybugs are small insects.
The picture shows us that ladybugs are red with black spots and have tiny legs.
So, the words gave us facts we can read, like what kind of animal it is.
And the picture gave us details we can see, like its color and shape.
Some things are hard to tell in words.
The exact color of an animal.
The shape of its spots. How tall it is.
Pictures show us those right away!
Sometimes, pictures and words in a book tell us different things.
Pictures often show us what something looks like or where it is.
Words can tell us names, feelings, or why something happened.
It's important to notice if the picture or the words are giving you new information.
You are now a pro at telling the difference between what pictures and words tell us!
Fact books have special parts called text features.
They help you find facts fast.
Let us meet them!
Headings are big words at the top of a section.
They tell you what that part is about.
Bold words are important vocabulary.
A caption tells you about a picture.
An index is at the back. It lists topics with page numbers.
Use the index like a shortcut!
Here is a helpful trick.
Before reading, flip through. Look at headings and pictures.
Now you are ready to find info fast!

lessons.title: Why Did the Author Write This?

steps.ttsScript: Every author writes for a reason.
We call that the author's purpose.
Usually it is to teach, to entertain, or to convince.
Fact books want to teach us.
They share facts, steps, and pictures that help us learn.
Stories entertain us. They make us laugh, cry, or wonder.
Some texts try to convince. They give reasons to agree with the author.
Here is a helpful trick.
When you finish, ask: why did the author write this?
Now you are ready to spot author purpose!
In fact books, pictures are not just decoration.
They show what words might not be able to say easily.
Let us see how!
A diagram shows parts of something.
Arrows and labels point to each part.
Easier to see than to read!
A map shows where things are.
Photos show real things close up.
Together they make facts come alive!
Here is a helpful trick.
When you see a picture, ask: how does this match the text?
Now you are ready to use pictures to understand facts!

currentSlides.heading: Match It Up!
currentSlides.forkPrompt: Match the fact to its picture

steps.ttsScript: Two texts on the same topic teach you more than one.
Each author picks different details to share.
Look for main points both books share. Those are the core facts.
Notice what each book shares that the other does not.
Different angles give you a fuller picture.
Here is a helpful trick.
Draw a T-chart. Same on one side. Different on the other.
Now you are ready to compare two texts!
Look! Fact books are full of real, true things.
They can be about anything. Bugs, planets, food, weather.
Let us learn how to enjoy fact books all year.
Pick fact books about things you love.
Love dinosaurs? Read about dinosaurs! Love space? Read about space!
When you love the topic, learning is fun.
Fact books have pictures, labels, and big words at the top.
Slow down and look at each one.
Pictures teach you facts the words might not say.
Here is a helpful trick.
Pick a new topic each week. You will discover something cool!
Now you are ready to read fact books all year!
Have you ever wondered who makes the fact books you read? Let's find out!
Every fact book has two important people — the author and the illustrator!
The author writes the WORDS. They chose all the facts for you!
The illustrator draws the PICTURES. They show you what the words say!
Together, they teach you everything in the book!
Let's try one together! Here's a fact book about bugs.
The book is called All About Beetles.
Who wrote the words? The author!
Who drew the pictures? The illustrator drew them!
The author writes the words and the illustrator draws the pictures. You found them both!
Look at this book about space. Who wrote it?
Right there on the cover — by Dr. Mia Orion! That's the author's name.
Dr. Orion wants us to learn about planets and rockets. That's her message!
Look at this book about jungle animals. Who drew the pictures?
Right there on the cover — pictures by Leo Bright! That's the illustrator's name.
Leo drew lions, tigers, and monkeys so we could see the jungle animals!
When you read a fact book, ask yourself three questions!
First ask: Who wrote it? That tells you the AUTHOR!
Next ask: Who drew the pictures? That tells you the ILLUSTRATOR!
Last ask: What are they teaching me? That's the MESSAGE!
Those three questions help you understand any fact book!
You're awesome at finding authors, illustrators, and their messages!
Let's practice figuring out who wrote the book, who drew the pictures, and what they want us to learn!
Reading a little every day is like a superpower.
The more stories and poems you read, the stronger your reading gets.
Let us see how to read all year long.
Pick stories about different things.
Funny ones. Scary ones. Adventure ones. Poems too!
New stories teach you new words and new ideas.
Sometimes a story has tricky words or long sentences.
That is a good thing! Growing readers try hard books.
When you need help, ask a grown-up or friend. That is smart!
Here is a helpful trick.
Pick a time to read every day. Bedtime, after lunch, or right when you wake up.
Now you are ready to enjoy stories all year long!
Did you know there are two big kinds of books?
Story books tell made-up stories.
Fact books give us real information.
Story books are full of adventures.
They have characters, a setting, and events that someone imagined.
Dragons, talking animals, magic. Anything goes in a story book!
Fact books teach us about the real world.
Animals, planets, weather, history. All true things!
Fact books often have photos, diagrams, and labels.
Here is a helpful trick.
Could this really happen in real life? Fact book. Made up? Story book!
Now you are ready to practice telling them apart!
Every story has a storyteller.
Sometimes it is a character in the story. Sometimes it is a voice outside.
Let us learn how to tell!
If the story uses the word I, a character is telling it.
Listen. I went to the store with my mom.
steps.displayText: I went to the store with my mom.

steps.ttsScript: The person saying I is the one telling the story. We call that first person.
If the story uses he, she, or they, a voice outside is telling it.
Listen. Sam ran to the park. He played on the swings.
steps.displayText: Sam ran to the park. He played on the swings.

steps.ttsScript: Someone is watching Sam and telling us. That is the narrator.
Here is a helpful trick.
Look at the first sentence. Does it say I, or does it say he, she, or they?
Now you are ready to spot the storyteller!
Pictures in a book are not just decoration.
They give us clues about characters, places, and feelings!
Let us learn what to look for.

currentSlides.heading: A Happy Face Tells a Lot

steps.ttsScript: Look at this picture.
A girl with a big smile, holding a trophy.
steps.displayText: A girl with a big smile, holding a trophy.

steps.ttsScript: How does she probably feel? Happy! Proud!
The picture told us. We did not even need words.
Pictures also show us where and when.
Snow on the ground. Kids in coats and hats. What season is it?
steps.displayText: Snow on the ground. Kids in coats and hats.

steps.ttsScript: Winter! The picture showed us.
Here is a helpful trick.
Look at the picture and read the words. Both tell the story together.
Now you are ready to practice using pictures as clues!
Two stories can be alike in some ways and different in others.
We compare to see what is the same.
We contrast to see what is different.
Story one. A bear looks for honey.
Story two. A bee makes honey.
What is the same? Both are about honey!
What is different? One finds it, one makes it.
Story one. Amy is brave and climbs a mountain.
steps.displayText: Amy is brave and climbs a mountain.

steps.ttsScript: Story two. Bob is brave and swims a lake.
steps.displayText: Bob is brave and swims a lake.

steps.ttsScript: Same? Both are brave adventures!
Different? One climbs, one swims.
Here is a helpful trick.
Ask, what do both stories share? Then ask, what is special about each one?
Now you are ready to practice comparing stories!
Pictures are part of the story too.
They show details the words might not say.
Let us use them together!
The words might say: it was cold.
The picture shows snow, bare trees, and a deer in a coat.
Now we know it is winter!
The picture shows how the character feels.
A huge smile means excited or proud.
Crossed arms and a frown? Maybe angry or upset.
Here is a helpful trick.
When you read, pause on each picture. Ask, what does it add?
Now you are ready to use pictures to understand stories!
